Robinhood is meanwhile working with the Treasury Department to launch and maintain an app for the government’s new Trump Accounts program, which aims to provide children with tax-deferred investment accounts. And Robinhood offered prediction market contracts on matters involving the federal government, including government shutdowns, which OPM monitors . Kupor also reported exercising stock call options and selling between $3 million and $12 million worth of stock in Okta Inc. on June 18, according to ethics records. Okta, an identity verification tech company, is a federal government contractor . In an ethics agreement Kupor signed last year prior to his Senate confirmation, he agreed to take steps to “avoid any actual or apparent conflict of interest” and divest of dozens of personal investments. He also resigned from various corporate posts and positions. In a statement to NOTUS, OPM spokesperson McLaurine Pinover said Kupor “went through a full financial review with [the Office of Government Ethics] prior to his confirmation hearing and agreed to all divestitures and recusals proposed by OGE. Neither Okta nor Robinhood were suggested by OGE as divestitures since OPM has no financial relationship with either company.” The OGE declined to comment on Kupor’s personal investments. The agency’s published “conflicts of interest considerations” guidance states that “an employee who owns stock options is prohibited from participating personally and substantially in any particular matter that the employee knows would have a direct and predictable effect on the financial interests of the issuer of the underlying security.” Walter Shaub, who served as director of the Office of Government Ethics from to , said Trump has set an “anything goes” standard for how his top lieutenants can invest their personal assets. The president reported thousands of stock and bond trades during the past year and has routinely engaged in private crypto and other business ventures since returning to the White House in . “It has seemed to me that the president’s appointees are doing a whole lot of buying and selling investments. That’s not something you saw happening much in the past Democratic or Republican administrations,” Shaub said. “The problem is that letting presidential appointees play the market is a recipe for disaster,” Shaub . “There’s no way for the public to know which government decisions are made because they’ll be lucrative for administration officials instead of being made because they’re what’s best for the American people.” In recent months, several top Trump administration officials have made notable personal financial trades or deals while serving in public office. They include FBI Director Kash Patel , Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee , Ambassador to Italy Tilman Fertitta , Federal Highway Administration Administrator Sean McMaster , U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro , Small Business Administration Administrator Kelly Loeffler , former U.S. Agency for Global Media leader Kari Lake , Department of Homeland Security Undersecretary Pedro Allende , Environmental Protection Agency Assistant Administrator Douglas Troutman and former Department of Health and Human Services general counsel Mike Stuart .

title: ABC Fires Back at FCC Over ‘Attempted Censorship’
author: Raymond Fernández
summary: The network argued the Trump administration is retaliating against it for exercising its First Amendment rights.
content: “We can do this the easy way or the hard way,” FCC chairman Brendan Carr told ABC in September . “These companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.” Aaron Schwartz/Sipa USA via AP ABC News accused the Trump administration of attempting to censor the network in a new regulatory filing responding to the Federal Communications Commission's decision to review the broadcast licenses of its owned-and-operated television stations years before they are set to expire. The television network, which has been targeted by the FCC because of its programming and on-air comments , argues the administration “is retaliating against ABC for the exercise of its First Amendment rights.” “The retaliation against ABC is a signal to every media company in the country: accommodate the Administration’s view of what news coverage should look like or pay the price,” the -page filing said. The administration first singled out the network for allegedly violating equal employment opportunity law in March . Later that year, the administration took issue with comments made by late night host Jimmy Kimmel, after which Trump called for Kimmel’s firing. “We can do this the easy way or the hard way,” FCC chairman Brendan Carr told ABC in September . “These companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.” The station’s renewal cycle was not set to begin until , according to the FCC. Some of the stations the FCC wants to review are based in cities including New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago. Individual viewers have submitted more than , comments concerning the “untimely” license renewal request — 96% of which are supportive of ABC, the network says. Carr’s actions have sparked concern even among some of its staunchest allies. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) described Carr’s comments to the network as “dangerous as hell.” Former FCC chairs who served under Democratic and Republican administrations also bashed his leadership, calling his decision to review licensing agreements “an assault on free speech.” “The Chairman has prejudged the outcome of this proceeding and that the Commission may assert the power to terminate the stations’ licenses early,” the former chairs wrote in a letter to the FCC on Tuesday. “All this betrays that this proceeding is pretext for the Chairman’s continued campaign of suppressing disfavored speech.” In December , ABC settled a $15 million lawsuit Trump filed against the network over a “This Week” segment in which the host asserted that the president had been found liable for raping writer E. Jean Carroll. A jury found Trump liable for sexual abuse in May .

title: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie Returns Donation From Pardoned Republican Megadonor
author: Avani Kalra
summary: The Republican congressman from Pennsylvania received a contribution from Adam Kidan three days before Trump pardoned him.
content: President Donald Trump and Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pennsylvania) appear on stage together during a campaign event on June 23, , in Macungie, Pennsylvania. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pennsylvania) returned a donation to a man convicted of fraud in connection with the Jack Abramoff lobbying scandal following reporting that President Donald Trump pardoned him just three days after the contribution. NOTUS reported Wednesday that Adam Kidan donated $2, to Mackenzie’s leadership PAC on June 30, according to Federal Election Commission records. Trump had traveled to Mackenzie’s district on June 23 to campaign alongside the congressman. Trump pardoned Kidan on July 3. Mackenzie’s returned donation was first reported by The Morning Call . A spokesperson for Mackenzie did not immediately respond to requests for comment from NOTUS about returning the contribution but told The Morning Call that the congressman returned the donation “to avoid even an appearance of impropriety.” Arnaud Armstrong, a spokesperson for Mackenzie, previously told NOTUS that Mackenzie “has never advocated for a pardon from the President on anyone’s behalf.” Kidan donated to Mackenzie’s leadership PAC, a fundraising vehicle often used to contribute money to other like-minded candidates and political committees, and it is the most recent donation Kidan has made, according to FEC records. AdamKidan ( , AR: 0.66)Mackenzie, who represents Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District, is facing off against Democrat Bob Brooks in one of the most contested House races in the country, which the Cook Political Report ranks a “toss up.” Kidan served more than two years in prison beginning in after pleading guilty to conspiracy and wire fraud. He is a notable campaign donor in Pennsylvania and throughout the nation, contributing to Republicans locked in other contested Pennsylvania races, such as Reps. Rob Bresnahan, Brian Fitzpatrick and Scott Perry. He has donated millions of dollars to Republican causes over the years and gave more than $ , to Trump-affiliated committees ahead of the election cycle, federal records show. Kidan and Abramoff were ordered to pay $ million in restitution as part of their sentencing. It remains unclear whether Kidan paid the full amount, and Trump’s pardon is likely to erase any remaining obligations.

title: Exclusive: What Got Cut From Fauci’s Diary
author: Evan McMorris-Santoro, Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
content: Katie Miller and Stephen Miller smile as they walk past reporters at the White House on Friday, July 31, . Alex Brandon/AP Today’s notice: The stuff redacted from Fauci’s journal in the last few days will surprise you. Todd Blanche’s confirmation vote delayed. Centrist Democrat vs. Centrist Democrat in Michigan. More green spending. And: Chris Murphy wants answers on the civics contest controversy. THE LATEST Anthony Fauci and the Millers: Former Trump administration official Katie Miller , wife of top White House adviser Stephen Miller , is publicly one of Fauci’s harshest critics, joining in conservative calls for him to be imprisoned for his work during the COVID-19 pandemic. But NOTUS’ Margaret Manto reports that Fauci’s journal, released by Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky) ahead of yesterday’s blockbuster Senate hearing, reveals a different side to their relationship in the scary, early days of COVID. “Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone,” Fauci wrote of Katie Miller in an entry dated May 9, . The journal entry said, “I am calling katie frequently to check on her couple time per day. She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant.” In the entries, Fauci writes about providing medical advice to the family on several occasions, including when both Katie and Stephen contracted the virus. These entries were public, but now they’re not. They were in Paul’s original document dump, but some entries were heavily redacted at some point between their release Saturday and yesterday. The original documents mentioned Katie Miller 56 times, while the redacted documents mentioned her 37 times. Paul’s office did not respond to a request for comment. Katie’s explanation: She told Margaret yesterday that she purposely gave Fauci the impression that she was friendly with him so that he “did not leak against me or my husband.” “He was not my doctor. He was not my friend,” Katie told NOTUS. “He was a work colleague who called me for work purposes, and in the course of a phone call, you would discuss other things.” Open tabs: Re-Redistricting Yields a More Republican, Less Elastic House Map (Cook Report); Trump and DOJ ask SCOTUS to toss $83M defamation verdict in E. Jean Carroll case (AP); St. Paul mayor under investigation for sexual harassment after alleged ‘Weiner Wednesday’ text (KSTP); Democrats Can’t Recast Ballots Ahead of Wisconsin Gubernatorial Primary (NOTUS); More Migrant Kids Are Getting Removal Orders. Some Could Lose Their Attorneys Too. (NOTUS) From the Hill Todd Blanche’s confirmation grinds to a halt. For now, at least. The Senate Judiciary Committee has delayed a vote on the acting attorney general’s nomination to drop the acting from the title. Republican Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas still haven’t agreed to vote for Blanche. An actual “no” vote from either of them would probably tank the nomination, NOTUS’ Al Weaver writes . Senate Democrats don’t want a shutdown this fall: Several key caucus members told NOTUS this week that they are open to a short-term stopgap spending measure to get through the election, our Stephen Neukam and Igor Bobic report . Sen. Katie Britt (R-Alabama), an appropriator, said she is “cautiously optimistic” about the status of government funding talks. From the campaign trail “I think we might be about to shoot ourselves in the head on this one,” a Michigan Democratic strategist tells NOTUS’ Alex Roarty of the mess centrists have made for themselves in the state’s 7th Congressional District. It’s a top pickup opportunity for Democrats, but the establishment is torn between two candidates, former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam and onetime Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink , and risks splitting the vote and handing the nomination to progressive William Lawrence , co-founder of the oft-controversial activism group Sunrise Movement. Neither centrist has shown any sign of backing down. Progressives are filling up another bowl of popcorn as it all unfolds. First on NOTUS: More green money for Democrats. The super PAC affiliated with the League of Conservation Voters plans to spend $50 million on the midterms, NOTUS’ Elena Schneider reports . The money will go to help Democratic candidates across the country by targeting voters who feel the affordability pinch, the group told Elena. Traditional environmentalism has taken a back seat in Democratic messaging this cycle, and the LCV-affiliated PAC is the latest green group to shift their focus to an affordability pitch. Last week, we told you about a Pennsylvania buy from NRDC Action Votes , the political spending group affiliated with the Natural Resources Defense Council, taking a similar approach. When is a corporate donation not a corporate donation? The Democrats’ pick to challenge Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R-Pennsylvania) in November is running on a pledge against money from corporate PACs. But campaign finance documents show that money is still flowing in for Paige Cognetti , the mayor of Scranton — just indirectly, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra reports . And it’s reviving the long-debated question about PAC money and its role in politics. Money from noncorporate PAC money is pouring into Congetti’s campaign, but those noncorporate PACs are frequently bankrolled by their corporate partners. Take for example Democratic Sen. Chris Coons ’ Blue Hen Federal PAC. Cognetti has taken $5, from that PAC, which has ties to corporations such as Visa, FedEx and Google. title: Paige Cognetti Refuses Corporate PAC Money. But Some Is Arriving Indirectly.
author: Avani Kalra
summary: The Democratic candidate in a hot Pennsylvania congressional race has accepted money from political groups that are themselves funded by corporate PACs.
content: Scranton, Pennsylvania, Mayor Paige Cognetti, a Democrat, is running in a tight race for Congress against Rep. Rob Bresnahan, a Republican. Matt Rourke/AP Paige Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton, Pennsylvania, who Democrats hope will unseat Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan this November, has repeatedly pledged not to take money from corporate political action committees as a candidate or lawmaker. “No Corporate PAC Money. As a candidate and member of Congress I will reject the influence of special interests,” Cognetti wrote on her campaign website. But federal campaign finance filings show Cognetti has accepted donations from numerous political committees that themselves are awash in cash from corporate PACs, including money from defense contractor Boeing, banking giant JPMorgan Chase and insurance company UnitedHealthcare. Many of the non-corporate political committees supporting Cognetti are leadership PACs operated by Democratic federal lawmakers to boost their party’s congressional candidates. During her campaign to represent Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District, Cognetti has, for example, taken $5, from Blue Hen Federal PAC , a committee sponsored by Sen. Chris Coons (D-Delaware). Coons’ committee has received hundreds of thousands of dollars this election cycle from a who’s who of corporate and trade association PACs tied to companies such as Visa , FedEx , Pfizer , Northrop Grumman , Eli Lilly , Google , McKinsey and Fox News parent Fox Corp. , among several dozen others. Cognetti’s campaign has also received $4, from the campaign committee of House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark, which itself is partly bankrolled by numerous corporate PACs, including those sponsored by Delta Air Lines , Verizon , Allstate Insurance and law and lobbying firm Alston & Bird . Cognetti took money from dozens of these leadership PACs that report significant corporate contributions — including the PACs of Rep. Ted Lieu, the House Democratic Caucus vice chair, and Rep. Nancy Pelosi, the former speaker. “Paige is the only candidate in this race who does not accept donations from corporate PACs, supports a federal ban on corporate PAC donations, and will never be handed a corporate check in exchange for special access or political favors,” Emma Mustion, the campaign’s communications director, said. “The reason for her pledge is simple: Paige is independent and doesn’t work for anybody but the people of Northeastern Pennsylvania.” Cognetti’s pledge to reject corporate PAC money has become a key feature of her campaign, and is cited in endorsements from advocacy groups such as End Citizens United and lawmakers including Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona). Campaign finance and other money matters are key issues in the race between Cognetti and Bresnahan. Cognetti has repeatedly hit Bresnahan, who accepts direct corporate PAC money, for his once-prolific stock trading — the multimillionaire with his own helicopter made more than individual stock trades during , according to federal records. Among them, he traded stock in companies that manage Medicaid just before the House took its first vote on Republicans’ sweeping tax cut bill that slashed the program. He has also personally invested in artificial intelligence companies before advocating for data centers . NOTUS previously reported that Bresnahan abruptly stopped trading stocks earlier this year . At the time, a spokesperson said a financial institution managed Bresnahan’s stock trades. “Only a slick politician like Paige Cognetti would make a promise to reject corporate PAC money a centerpiece of her campaign only to find a loophole to accept it,” Samantha Bullock, a spokesperson for Bresnahan’s campaign, said in a statement to NOTUS. RobBresnahan1 ( , AR: 1.50)Federal records show Cognetti had $3.4 million cash on hand, besting Bresnahan’s $2.6 million war chest, as of June 30. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the race between Bresnahan and Cognetti as a toss-up. National Republicans and Democrats alike consider the race critical to winning a House majority in . Cognetti, for her part, continues to run on an anti-corruption platform that includes banning members of Congress from trading individual stocks, instituting term limits for federal lawmakers, withholding lawmakers’ pay throughout government shutdowns and prohibiting members of Congress from making bets in prediction markets. Other candidates have been criticized in the past for accepting similar contributions. Democrat Abigail Spanberger, now the governor of Virginia, campaigned on rejecting corporate PAC money while running for Congress in — and was slammed at the time for taking money from leadership PACs.

title: Redacted Fauci Diary Entries Depict Him Personally Helping Katie Miller
author: Margaret Manto
summary: Katie Miller, who has since called for infectious disease doctor Anthony Fauci to be jailed, has said Fauci’s diary entries are self-aggrandizing.
content: Anthony Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergies and Infectious Diseases who served as the of the Trump administration’s COVID-19 response. Samuel Corum/Sipa USA via AP Former White House official and conservative influencer Katie Miller heralded the release of Anthony Fauci’s diaries as a bombshell discovery that outed him as a calculating attention-seeker. “The most disturbing part of Fauci’s diary — is what he decided to memorialize versus what he kept out of his diary,” she wrote in a post on X on Monday. “It’s almost like he knew this diary would one day become public. He wanted to cast himself as the hero, as famous, as the savior.” Katie Miller, who is married to Trump adviser and White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, has called for Fauci to be jailed. She derided Fauci’s appearance in front of the Senate Wednesday, questioning why he repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment. And she’s said he caused “decades of harm” to children as a leader of the federal government’s COVID-19 response. Since-redacted excerpts from Fauci’s diary indicate his relationship with Katie Miller was not always this way. In entries dated to , Fauci’s diary suggests he had a close relationship with Katie Miller, who was Vice President Mike Pence’s communications director at the time and heavily involved in the White House’s COVID-19 response. Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul, a longtime critic of Fauci’s, published more than 1, pages of the infectious disease doctor’s diary Saturday. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told Fox News that he handed the entries over to Senate Republicans after finding them on government servers. Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergies and Infectious Diseases who served as the of the Trump administration’s COVID-19 response, writes about providing medical advice to Katie and Stephen Miller. He writes that he counseled the family after Katie Miller tested positive for COVID-19 while pregnant in , when Stephen Miller tested positive and when their newborn child experienced a medical episode later that year. “I am calling katie frequently to check on her couple time per day. She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant. Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone,” Fauci wrote in an entry dated May 9, . In another entry, Fauci writes that he called the doctors of Miller’s child directly to discuss the infant’s medical care. Some of the entries detailing Fauci’s interactions with Miller were made public in the initial document dump, but were later redacted. A NOTUS analysis comparing the originally posted document and the document available Wednesday afternoon show many of the redactions included sections of the diary recounting Fauci’s interactions with the Millers. The original document mentioned Katie Miller 56 times, while the redacted document mentioned her 37 times. Katie Miller requested that NOTUS not disclose the details of her child’s medical history and said Paul’s office published them without her knowledge or permission. Paul’s office did not respond to a request for comment. She said that while she and Fauci were in regular contact during the initial COVID-19 response and would occasionally discuss nonwork matters, her opinion of him at the time was that he was “incredibly self-centered and sought to promote himself above the good of the people.” “He was not my doctor. He was not my friend. He was a work colleague who called me for work purposes, and in the course of a phone call, you would discuss other things,” Miller told NOTUS. She said she purposely gave Fauci the impression that she was friendly with him so that he “did not leak against me or my husband.” “I understood who he was, and I understood how to manage somebody like him,” she said. She pointed to a passage in Fauci’s diaries where he describes agreeing with Stephen Miller on the need for border restrictions to prevent the spread of COVID-19. “How did Stephen Miller manage to get Dr. Fauci there?” she asked rhetorically. “It’s understanding how to communicate with somebody who wants to put themselves above others.” In recent years, Katie Miller served as the media representative for Kennedy during the presidential transition and as an aide to Elon Musk’s DOGE initiative. Since leaving the administration, she has hosted Kennedy on her podcast. She’s also talked about not vaccinating her youngest child. Fauci’s diary entries depict Katie Miller as a frequent ally while the Coronavirus Task Force was active and someone he relied on to help sort out issues with Trump and Pence. “katie Miller is great (tough, smart,but great),” Fauci wrote on March 25, . Fauci did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Katie Miller, in turn, went to him when her husband tested positive for COVID-19 in the fall of , Fauci wrote. After Stephen Miller tested positive, Fauci writes, he spoke to Katie multiple times as she was traveling to her parents’ home in Texas. “Spoke to her at Houston airport and after she landed,” he wrote in an entry dated October 6, . “Am on phone frequently with katie and Stephen,” Fauci wrote on December 31, . Fauci’s depiction of their relationship in stands in sharp contrast to the opinions Miller has expressed about Fauci in recent years. “From the first day of the COVID task force, Dr. Fauci cared more about virtue signaling than science,” Katie Miller wrote in a post on X. For some, including former members of the Trump administration , Fauci has come to symbolize government overreach and hubris in the wake of the pandemic. He became the subject of conspiracy theories claiming the federal government covered up the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic and widespread negative reactions to the vaccine. Neither theory has been supported by evidence. Nevertheless, in anticipation of attempts to prosecute the former health official, former President Joe Biden issued a preemptive pardon for any offenses Fauci may have committed “related to his service as Director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, as a member of the White House Coronavirus Task Force or the White House” before leaving office. Paul, an outspoken critic of Fauci’s, compelled him to appear before the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Government Affairs Wednesday. During the hearing, Fauci, now 85, said in his opening statement that Paul had an “unhinged obsession” with putting him behind bars. “Given Senator Paul’s obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution, his repeated slanderous comments about me, and recently his publicly releasing my unredacted personal diary aimed at embarrassing and intimidating me, the only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this Committee is to get me to say something that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars,’” Fauci said. Miller herself has also called for Fauci’s prosecution. When former Director of National Security Tulsi Gabbard released documents last month she claimed showed that Fauci directed funds toward “dangerous” biological research in China, Miller wrote on X , “When asked this question in the Situation Room during the COVID Task Force meetings six years ago, Dr. Fauci said no. Dr. Fauci used the government's medical establishment to push an agenda that protected and promoted himself at the expense of the American people. His autopen pardon should be trashed, and he should be in jail.” That’s a stark departure from the relationship Fauci wrote about in his diary. “katie Miller and I laugh at each other in the Sit Room,” he wrote on May 6, .

title: Major D.C. Law Firm Details Theft From Political Committee
author: Jenna Monnin
summary: The Arnold & Porter PAC told federal regulators a thief stole paper checks from mailboxes in Washington’s upscale Cleveland Park neighborhood.
content: A thief stole political contribution checks from a mailbox in Washington, D.C., the political action committee of law firm Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer LLP told the Federal Election Commission. Kirby Lee/AP A thief stole, then altered, multiple political contribution checks sent through the mail by the political action committee of a major Washington-based law firm, according to a new letter to federal regulators NOTUS reviewed. The unidentified thief stole two of the checks from a batch of political donation payments the Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer LLP’s PAC mailed in D.C.’s upscale Cleveland Park neighborhood on Nov. 24, . Arnold & Porter subsequently increased its security protocols, enrolling in Truist bank’s fraud inspector program, which generates an email to the committee “every time a payment is debited from its bank account,” allowing the PAC to dispute any unauthorized payments. Arnold & Porter’s Wednesday letter to the Federal Election Commission provides these and other new details about the theft, which NOTUS first revealed in June . And it arrives amid a rash of thefts involving federal political committees, including revelations this week involving the cash-strapped Democratic National Committee and the Senate campaign of Michigan Republican Mike Rogers . The law firm’s PAC described the unknown party that carried out the theft as a “criminal actor” who intercepted and washed the checks — changing the payee and dollar amount. Arnold & Porter’s treasurer, Nicholas L. Townsend, told the FEC that the thief altered one check intended for the campaign committee of Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-New York). After stealing the check, the thief changed the written value — $1, — to $40, and made it out to "Gleora Agoj" with "Advisory Asistant fee" written on the memo line. The name on the check does not appear to be affiliated with Arnold & Porter. The Meeks campaign never received the funds, according to the memo. Another check addressed to the American Mosaic PAC, a committee focused on increasing diversity in Congress, was altered from $2, to $20, . The Arnold & Porter PAC discovered “that at least one check, and possibly more, had not been received by the intended recipients” and put “stop-payment requests” on the disbursements to Meeks’ campaign and the American Mosaic PAC. The law firm, which is headquartered in D.C., called Truist on May 1 after it noticed multiple unauthorized payments and the “two suspicious check deposits pending” while compiling its monthly financial report to the FEC. The bank assured Arnold & Porter that the committee’s account would not be charged, but the $40, was still taken from the PAC’s funds. The $20, check was never honored by the bank because of the stop-payment order, Townsend told the FEC. The Arnold & Porter committee ultimately recouped the $40, in stolen funds from the fraudulent check and an additional $2, unauthorized payments through the bank. ArnoldPorter ( , AR: 1.41)Following the theft, the committee told the FEC it had taken several steps, including enrollment in its bank’s fraud detection program, to address any security or information gaps in its payment processes. “The Committee also submitted an incident report to the U.S. Postal Service stating that someone was stealing mail in the neighborhood,” Townsend wrote. Arnold & Porter did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the memo. Check fraud is generally on the rise across the nation, with suspicious activity reports, or documents filed by financial institutions to report suspected violations of the law, nearly doubling from to , according to the FBI .

title: Maine Makes Its Legal Case for Kneecapping Super PACs
author: Taylor Giorno
summary: But in federal court today, free speech advocates defended the right of political donors to make unlimited contributions to certain political groups.
content: The state of Maine and an allied nonprofit organization want to cap unlimited contributions to super PACs and other big-money political groups. Caroline Brehman/CQ Roll Call via AP In a federal appeals court in Boston on Wednesday, free speech advocates sparred with the state of Maine and an allied nonprofit organization that want to cap unlimited contributions to super PACs and other big-money political groups. The state of Maine and Equal Citizens, a nonprofit group founded by Harvard law professor and erstwhile presidential candidate Larry Lessig, are fighting to restore a Maine law capping individual contributions to certain big-spending political groups, such as super PACs, at $5, . They’re hoping to take their case all the way to the Supreme Court. But they stiff resistance Wednesday from opponents who argue that spending by outside political groups — groups that raise and spend money to influence elections but are not allowed to coordinate directly with candidates — is a protected form of political speech. Two super PACs, Dinner Table Action and For Our Future, sued Maine state election officials — successfully — to stop the law, which Maine voters overwhelmingly approved in , from going into effect. “The American people have a First Amendment right to assemble and to associate, to engage in political speech, and particularly election-related speech, free of infringement from many laws,” Charles "Chip" Miller, a senior attorney at the Institute for Free Speech, which is representing the super PACs, said Wednesday. “That is what we're here talking about today. That's what independent expenditures are. It's the association of individuals to get together to speak.” But Americans across the political spectrum overwhelmingly believe there is too much money in U.S. politics, according to recent polling by Politico , Pew Research Center and others . The midterm election is expected to be the most expensive non-presidential cycle on record, with well-funded super PACs — including the president’s MAGA Inc. and those controlled by cryptocurrency, artificial intelligence and sports-betting industries — poised to play a major role in shaping the election landscape. Maine is one of several states that’s attempted to limit the amount of money flowing into their elections, which has exploded since , when the Supreme Court greenlit unlimited spending by outside groups in its Citizens United v. FEC decision. “This case presents a single question: When the people of Maine decided, by the largest vote in the state's -year history, that unlimited super PAC contributions were corrupting their elections, did the First Amendment leave them powerless? It did not,” Neal Katyal, a partner at Milbank LLP, who successfully argued against President Donald Trump’s tariffs at the Supreme Court earlier this year, said during oral arguments Wednesday. Lessig previously told the Maine Morning Star he had expected a legal challenge, and Equal Citizens joined the case to defend the contribution limits. Lessig’s stated goal is to get the case to the Supreme Court, which he argues hasn’t grappled directly with the constitutionality of unlimited political contributions. A few months after the Citizens United decision, a federal appeals court in D.C. applied the Supreme Court ruling to another case called SpeechNow.org v. FEC. The court ruled then that contribution limits, not just spending limits, were lawful, as did other appeals courts — and this is the precedent Maine and Equal Citizens are targeting. “The strategy is to get this case to the Supreme Court with the First Circuit coming into contradiction with the precedents of other Circuits including the Second, Fifth, Seventh, Ninth, Tenth — and, most importantly, the DC Circuit,” Maia Cook, Equal Citizens’ executive director, wrote in a statement to NOTUS. In a written statement to NOTUS ahead of oral argument, Miller said the Maine ballot measure “strikes at the heart of the First Amendment by severely limiting political speech.” “There is no legitimate government interest in limiting contributions to groups that make only independent expenditures,” Miller wrote. The odds that the case makes it to the Supreme Court would rise if the federal appeals court sides with Maine and Equal Citizens, which would create a tantalizing “circuit split” for the court. Last July, a U.S. magistrate judge stopped Maine from enforcing the law, which she called “unconstitutional on its .” The federal appeals court is expected to rule in November or December, although there’s no official timeline for releasing the decision. Even if the case gets to the Supreme Court, however, Maine faces an uphill battle. Conservative justices have sympathized with arguments that super PACs erode the power of political parties, in part fueling their decision last month to strike down coordination limits between political party committees and candidates. But that doesn’t mean justices are willing to limit super PACs’ ability to spend as much money as they want to advocate for or against political candidates. “[D]onors can and do send their funds to Super PACs and other outside groups that have a First Amendment right to receive and spend unlimited money to support their independent political speech,” conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in the opinion last month.

title: Trump Teleprompter Operator at Center of Gambling Scandal Is Out of a Job
author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
summary: Gabriel Perez, who allegedly made roughly $ , betting on Trump’s speeches, was previously placed on unpaid leave.
content: It is unclear whether the White House fired Perez or if he resigned. Mark Schiefelbein/AP The teleprompter operator accused of unlawfully gambling on President Donald Trump’s speeches via a prediction marketplace is no longer employed by the White House. A White House official confirmed Wednesday that Gabriel Perez “no longer works in the federal government.” It is unclear whether the White House fired Perez or if he resigned. Perez allegedly placed bets on Kalshi that were flagged by the company’s surveillance team to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, according to Robert DeNault, the head of enforcement for Kalshi. “We have charged this individual and have been assisting regulators on this matter and provided evidence we collected, as we do in any referral,” DeNault said in a statement earlier this month. Perez, who is accused of making roughly $ , from the bets, has cooperated with federal investigators from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, a source familiar with the matter previously told NOTUS. Trump called the incident “deeply unfortunate,” White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said during a briefing on July 16. At the time, Perez had been placed on unpaid leave. Leavitt previously told NOTUS that no other White House staff are currently suspected of misconduct related to wagering on prediction markets. Lawmakers from both parties have advocated for legislation to prohibit federal elected officials and government employees from using insider information to place bets on prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket. In April, the Justice Department alleged that U.S. Army Master Sgt. Gannon Ken Van Dyke, who was involved in the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, used classified information to place a wager on Polymarket.

title: Megadonor Received Trump Pardon Three Days After Donation to Pennsylvania Congressman
author: Avani Kalra
summary: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie’s campaign says the lawmaker, who met with Trump days before, played no role in the pardon.
content: President Donald Trump and Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pennsylvania) appear on stage together during an event at a Mack Trucks facility on June 23, , in Macungie, Pennsylvania. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP President Donald Trump recently pardoned a major Republican donor three days after the man — a key figure in the Jack Abramoff fraud and lobbying scandal — made a political donation to Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pennsylvania), who’s facing one of the nation’s most contested House races. The megadonor, Adam Kidan, donated $2, to Mackenzie's leadership PAC on June 30, according to Federal Election Commission records. Trump traveled to Mackenzie’s eastern Pennsylvania district on June 23 to campaign with him. The president pardoned Kidan on July 3. Mackenzie’s office told NOTUS that the Republican congressman did not speak with the White House or Trump about the pardon, but it declined to answer questions about whether the congressman intends to keep Kidan’s donation. “Congressman Mackenzie has never advocated for a pardon from the President on anyone’s behalf,” Mackenzie spokesperson Arnaud Armstrong said in a statement. The White House and Kidan did not respond to NOTUS’ requests for comment. Mackenzie faces Democratic challenger Bob Brooks to represent Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District in what the Cook Political Report ranks as a “toss-up” race. In an email to NOTUS, Brooks campaign manager Jenna Kaufman said: “Three days after a convicted fraudster cut Ryan Mackenzie a massive campaign check, that same fraudster walked away with a presidential pardon. That is corruption in plain sight.” Kidan, who served about two-and-a-half years in prison in after pleading guilty to conspiracy and wire fraud, has donated millions to Republican causes over the years. He gave around $ , to Trump-affiliated committees during the election cycle, according to federal records, and has hosted fundraisers at Mar-a-Lago. AdamKidan ( , AR: 0.66)He has also contributed to a number of Republican campaigns throughout the midterms, including donations in to three swing-district House members from Pennsylvania: Rob Bresnahan, Brian Fitzpatrick and Scott Perry. He has also supported Pennsylvania Treasurer Stacy Garrity’s bid for governor in the state. In April, Kidan donated $7, to former Rep. Mike Rogers’ Senate bid in Michigan, $3, to Rep. Zach Nunn’s reelection in Iowa and $22, to Rep. Jim Jordan’s joint fundraising committee in Ohio, federal records show. Kidan’s donation to Mackenzie’s leadership PAC is his most recent federal political contribution on record, FEC records indicate. As part of his sentencing, Kidan and Abramoff were ordered to pay a total of $ million in restitution. It’s unclear whether Kidan paid the full amount, and Trump’s pardon is likely to erase any remaining financial obligations.

title: Inside the Push to Claw Back Graham Platner’s Campaign Money
author: Oriana González
summary: “Anything that we can do to try to take resources out of the hands of predators is worth it,” Cheyenne Hunt told NOTUS.
content: Robert F. Bukaty/AP Cheyenne Hunt watched Rep. Eric Swalwell use campaign funds for legal fees after sexual assault allegations chased him out of Congress. She decided to do something to not watch Graham Platner do the same. Hunt, a prominent activist and lawyer, launched her organization Reckoning Action in response to the accusations against Swalwell with the goal of ending misogyny in the workplace. After Swalwell, she knew she “had to get a little bit scrappier about how we do this,” Hunt told NOTUS in an interview. Ultimately, her organization decided to text Platner’s donors directly and teach them how they can get refunds from his campaign. “Anything that we can do to try to take resources out of the hands of predators is worth it,” Hunt said. Swalwell dropped out of the California governor’s race and resigned from Congress in early April after multiple women, including one of his former staffers , accused him of sexual assault . He has denied the accusations. Recent Federal Election Commission filings show that Swalwell spent $50, in campaign money on defense attorney Sara Azari, who specializes in “#metoo defense,” according to her website . Days after Swalwell resigned, Azari’s firm hired a private investigator who looked into the sexual assault allegations, NOTUS first reported . Platner, who ended his Senate campaign after being accused of sexual assault, presented a different challenge for Reckoning Action. The group sought legal advice and then informed the women who accused Platner of sexual assault “that there was a good chance that they were being watched and looked into,” Hunt said. “That is deeply unsettling for survivors after having to go through this incredibly invasive process of bringing that forward,” Hunt said. Platner had $1.7 million cash on hand at the end of last month, according to the most recent FEC data available, and Hunt was concerned that he could use that money “against these survivors.” Platner’s campaign did not respond to NOTUS’ request for comment. Reckoning Action sent automated texts signed by Hunt to donors with the following message: “If you donated to Graham Platner and feel betrayed, you’re not alone. You signed up to help elect a champion for freedom and equality and take back the Senate — not to fund a predator.” The text linked to a Reckoning Action website with instructions on how to get the refunds. Hunt told NOTUS that in the hours after they sent that text to “thousands” of donors on July 16, more than people visited the landing page. Many political donors use the platform ActBlue to contribute to Democratic campaigns. The site allows refunds within 90 days of the payment. Reckoning Action advised donors to contact ActBlue if the donation is older than 90 days or to contact Platner’s campaign directly to request a refund. The FEC does not allow campaign funds to be used for personal use, but it does allow that money to be used to cover legal expenses related to campaign activity, “where such expenses would not have occurred had the individual not been a candidate or officeholder,” according to its official website . There’s nothing that directly prohibits a candidate or an elected official from using campaign funds to fight sexual misconduct allegations. While Hunt and her organization reached out to Platner’s financial supporters, they were also in touch with lawmakers about changing the law. On Tuesday, Reps. Ro Khanna (D-California) and Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida) introduced the No Campaign Funded Cover-Ups Act, a bill that would prohibit candidates and elected officials on the federal level from using campaign money to cover costs related to sexual misconduct claims. It’s unclear whether the bill will become law, even with bipartisan support. “Survivors must be heard and respected. Our bipartisan legislation addresses a basic principle: money donated to support a political campaign should not become a personal legal-defense fund for alleged sexual misconduct,” Khanna said in a statement. Luna concurred in a statement: “If a candidate is accused of sexual assault, sexual abuse, or sexual harassment, campaign donations and legal expense funds should never become a personal bailout. If you commit sexual misconduct, you should foot the bill, not the donors who put their trust in you.” Platner has denied he sexually assaulted anyone. In an 11-minute video posted on X, he said the allegations were “false” and were “used by the political establishment” to kick him off the ballot in the Maine Senate race. The reactions from donors to Reckoning Action’s text were mixed. “Those that were negative definitely echoed the sentiments in his video,” Hunt said. “This concept of not really taking accountability, and that this was something that was happening to him versus a product of his own misconduct and his own lack of honesty. So that was hard.” “That’s just so disconnected from reality,” Hunt . But Platner’s many scandals have already made a dent in his campaign finances . His campaign committee refunded more than $43, to donors from late May to June 30, according to its most recent financial report. Those refunds happened at a time when he was dealing with reports of sexual text messages with women outside of his marriage. “I’m feeling pretty optimistic that we will have put another sizable dent in that campaign account,” Hunt said. The discussion around sexual misconduct in Congress has spurred lawmakers to create legislation to address sexual misconduct, beyond the Khanna-Luna bill. Rep. Jeff Crank (R-Colorado) recently introduced a resolution to prohibit House lawmakers from having romantic relationships with any House employee. The Republican and Democratic women’s caucuses are preparing to release recommendations after the August recess around overhauling how the House handles sexual misconduct allegations. Both Speaker Mike Johnson and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries have blessed the effort. “We’re protecting women. We’re protecting the staff,” Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, told reporters last week. “We’re protecting the really brilliant people who choose to come and work for us.”

title: The DNC Lost Nearly $29,000 to an Email Scammer Posing as Ken Martin
author: Dave Levinthal
summary: The Democratic National Committee caught the error, but only recovered a portion of the funds, an official said.
content: An email scammer received payment from a Democratic National Committee staffer after pretending to be Chair Ken Martin. Allison Robbert/AP A thief scammed the cash-strapped Democratic National Committee out of nearly $29, last year, according to interviews with committee officials and previously unreported federal records . In February , an unknown party sent a fraudulent email to a committee staffer pretending to be Chairman Ken Martin, a DNC official familiar with the matter confirmed to NOTUS. Martin had begun his tenure days before. The staffer, who is no longer at the DNC, made a payment to the fraudster. The DNC official said the committee caught the error within minutes and reported it to its financial institution — Wells Fargo, according to federal records — but could only recover $7, of the lost money. The theft is one of numerous high-profile swindles from prominent political committees — liberal and conservative alike — and comes as the DNC is facing a cash crunch that’s led it to put its Washington, D.C., headquarters up for collateral to obtain a $15 million line of credit . The DNC acknowledged what it called a “misdisbursement of Committee funds” in an August letter to the Federal Election Commission, saying it “was the result of fraudulent activity by an external third party.” It told regulators it would take “further steps to avoid similar events in the future.” The DNC also reported the matter to law enforcement, said the official, who stressed that the committee utilizes thorough training and security protocols to defend against fraud and other nefarious activity. “The DNC takes seriously our duty to protect the funds provided to us by millions of patriotic Americans chipping in to fund our mission,” spokesperson Mia Ehrenberg told NOTUS in a statement. “This was a one-off mistake that was promptly caught and addressed, and no similar issues have occurred since.” The stolen money represents a small fraction of what the DNC typically raises during an election cycle. But this election cycle has proven particularly challenging for the committee, which is operating in the red as Democrats attempt to win control of the House and Senate during November’s midterm elections. The DNC had about $16.3 million cash on hand versus about $18.5 million in debt through June 30, according to FEC records . The Republican National Committee, meanwhile, had more than $ .5 million cash on hand and no debt through June 30. Some Democratic activists have openly criticized Martin’s leadership and even called for his resignation , although most elected Democrats have remained silent on Martin or have offered their support for him. Dozens of federal political committees have suffered a financial loss this for a number of reasons — particularly cybertheft, mail fraud and embezzlement. In , the RNC lost $44, to fraudsters who went on a shopping spree at a coffee company and agricultural products supplier. More recently, Sens. John Thune (R-South Dakota), Chuck Schumer (D-New York), Mark Warner (D-Virginia), Tim Kaine (D-Virginia), Jerry Moran (R-Kansas), Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) have experienced campaign thefts. So, too, have the campaigns of House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) and Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York), Brittany Pettersen (D-Colorado) and Neal Dunn (R-Florida). Republican candidate Mike Rogers, a former congressman who’s running for the U.S. Senate in Michigan, lost $16, in campaign cash to a suspected cyberthief despite running on a platform that includes his experience “working with companies large and small to protect their data from criminals and bad-acting countries like China.” Thieves, scammers or embezzlers have also recently hit political committees for the National Venture Capital Association , Seafarers International Union , American Fintech Council , accounting giant KPMG and law firm Arnold & Porter .

title: Beshear Pushes McConnell to Resign or ‘Provide Proof’ He’s Fit to Serve
author: Jenna Monnin
summary: Sen. McConnell has not been seen in public since mid-June.
content: If McConnell steps down, a special election is required to fill his vacant Senate seat, according to a state law. J. Scott Applewhite/AP Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, gave Sen. Mitch McConnell an ultimatum on Monday: Provide more information about his ongoing health struggles and his ability to return to the Senate, or resign from office. “As Governor of the state you serve, I am calling on you to directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky and provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign,” Beshear wrote in a letter to the longtime senator’s office obtained by NOTUS. The letter, first reported by CNN , came on the heels of a statement released by McConnell Monday, announcing that he is still not cleared to return to the Senate and is focusing on “intense physical therapy.” The update included another picture of the senator and his wife, Elaine Chao, but did not include many details about his condition or an expected return date. McConnell that he would be unable to attend Kentucky’s Fancy Farm event this Saturday, which is the state’s long-standing bipartisan political rally. “There’s no place I’d rather be on the first Saturday in August than with the good people of western Kentucky, feasting on pork and mutton,” McConnell said in the statement. The Office of the Attending Physician stated that McConnell is continuing to recover, but Beshear took issue with the lack of details about the senator’s physical condition. “Even the attending physician’s written statement does not discuss your actual condition, including whether you can speak, reason, or carry out your duties as a senator,” Beshear wrote. The governor addressed the letter to McConnell but called on his Senate staff to be “honest and transparent” with Kentuckians if the senator is unable to reply. “I am addressing this letter to Senator McConnell under the assumption that he is capable of reading and responding verbally, and not incapacitated by means of consciousness or cognition,” Beshear wrote. “If the Senator is unable to respond for either of those or other conditions, consider this letter a demand for his Senate staff to be honest and transparent with the people of Kentucky.” McConnell’s office did not comment on the governor’s letter. Beshear sent the letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune along with an additional letter calling on him to investigate McConnell’s absence. “I think that's an issue, really, that’s between Sen. McConnell and the people of Kentucky,” Thune said when asked about the letter. “I’m not sure what [Beshear’s] prerogatives are in that case, but that’s where the issue should be resolved.” If McConnell steps down, a special election is required to fill his vacant Senate seat, according to a state law. A law would have allowed Beshear to choose a replacement for McConnell from a list of three Republicans provided by the outgoing senator. But the governor signaled that he might be willing to challenge the law. “There is a Kentucky constitutional provision that says that I appoint all state officers when there’s a vacancy,” Beshear told MS NOW earlier this month . “The question is, does that apply to federal offices? Well, before there was ever a law in Kentucky on how this would work, multiple appointments were made by governors, presumably under that provision.” McConnell has not been seen in public since his hospitalization on June 14. The senator’s office has released statements saying he is receiving medical treatment after suffering a fall and was "briefly unconscious” after the initial incident. As a survivor of childhood polio, McConnell has said that the illness still impacts his mobility. The senator had been seen using a wheelchair at the Capitol following a previous fall. This article has been updated with a comment from Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

title: Scammers Swindled Mike Rogers’ Senate Team Out of $16,700
author: Taylor Giorno
summary: The Republican candidate in Michigan reported the “fraudulent transaction” to federal regulators.
content: Former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers, who is running for the U.S. Senate in Michigan, had about $16, stolen from one of his political committees, according to federal records. Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Images Senate candidate Mike Rogers ’ joint fundraising committee got swindled this spring. Team Rogers, a joint fundraising committee for the Michigan Republican, flagged a “fraudulent transaction” worth about $16, in its most recent report to the Federal Election Commission. It’s the latest in a long line of financial crimes targeting political campaigns and committees. Alyssa Brouillet, a spokesperson for the Rogers campaign, told NOTUS the political committee had unknowingly paid a fraudulent invoice on April 21 after a vendor’s email had been hacked. “The invoice appeared to be received in the normal course of business and was approved for payment through normal channels,” Brouillet wrote in a statement. “Unfortunately, a week later, Team Rogers was notified that the vendor's email had been hacked and that the invoice was fraudulent.” Rogers, who is poised to the winner of the Democratic primary between Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, did not get the money back. Haley.Stevens.Abdul.ElSayed ( , AR: 1.50)“Despite an immediate request from Team Rogers, the bank was unable to recall the funds due to insufficient funds in the fraudulent account,” Brouillet wrote. She did not address a question from NOTUS asking if the committee had filed a police report or was taking legal action. The lost money is a fraction of the nearly $ , the committee reported spending between April and June. As of June 30, Team Rogers reported raising almost $1.5 million this election cycle, most of which it splits among Rogers’ campaign and leadership PAC, the National Republican Senatorial Committee and a pro-Rogers super PAC known as GLCF Inc. Unauthorized withdrawals from political campaigns and committees — often by trusted treasurers or advisers — have cost those groups millions of dollars since campaign finance regulators noticed an uptick in the crime two decades ago. Sens. Chuck Schumer (D-New York), Mark Warner (D-Virginia), Tim Kaine (D-Virginia), Jerry Moran (R-Kansas), Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) are among elected officials to experience recent campaign thefts. In January, the American Fintech Council’s PAC reported losing $2, after “fraudulent transactions,” money it was able to recoup. Meanwhile, two Democratic candidates accused their political consultant of embezzlement — allegations her lawyer denied when contacted by the Philadelphia Inquirer in March. In March, federal prosecutors charged a campaign treasurer of taking a combined $ , from two clients — a Maryland state delegate campaign and a community organization — to refinance a loan on his yacht. And in May, NOTUS reported that the daughter of the Seafarers International Union president allegedly embezzled hundreds of thousands of dollars from union-linked PACs.

title: DN-Seeing Red
author: Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva, Jenna Monnin
content: Caroline Brehman/AP Today’s notice: DNC’s collateral. Russia sanctions split Democratic hopefuls. Both parties are hoping to land the Latino vote. Why you're still being bombarded with pharmaceutical ads. And: The “army of one” staffing the pandemic preparedness office. THE LATEST Just 99 days before the midterms , the daggers are out for Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin, whose organization has $16 million on hand but $18 million in debt. The scrutiny increased after NOTUS’ Elena Schneider and Jasmine Wright reported the DNC put up its headquarters near the Capitol as collateral last year to obtain a $15 million line of credit. “After spending all of paying ’s bills, we are heading toward Election Day with a DNC now focused on how to pay off a mortgage on their headquarters instead of winning elections,” a DNC member told NOTUS. “Ken Martin is losing pace on a debt treadmill of his own creation. Sooner or later he’ll have to step off or be thrown off.” The DNC has used its facility for collateral previously — including in , and , a DNC official said. But Democrats aren’t too pleased that their national party is in the red so close to the midterms, especially as the Republican National Committee holds $ million in cash with no outstanding debts. “Ken gaslighting us about the DNC’s finances and not being transparent about the financial situation makes us doubt if he can oversee the DNC during the most important primary of our lifetime,” said another DNC member. If that weren't enough, sources told NOTUS that Martin has grown "paranoid" and is exhibiting "spiraling behavior." One incident in which sources said he threw a phone in the direction of an aide, first reported by The New York Times , isn’t helping. Rep. Sam LicCardo (D-California) put it bluntly on X last night: “Ken Martin must resign. As Democrats, we have become too captured by failing strategies. We must fail forward, and pivot. The urgency of this moment will not reward — and our children will not forgive — torpidity.” A DNC official pointed NOTUS to a recent Substack post in which Martin wrote that the committee has raised more money than the DNC ever has without a Democrat in the White House and said it “will be ready to win — everywhere, at every level.” Payments on the line of credit aren’t due until January. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said yesterday that he still has Martin’s back. “The chairman has my full support,” Jeffries told reporters, per NOTUS’ Kadia Goba. “We look forward to our continued partnership.” Speaking of Jeffries , he campaigned yesterday for Democrat Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District, though voters there told Kadia they weren’t sure Washington’s help was welcome. Open tabs: Republicans see ‘scary’ lack of enthusiasm among core voters ahead of midterms (WaPo); An Admiral’s Rise Reveals the Politics Driving Hegseth’s Pentagon (NYT); The shrinking world of former president Joe Biden (WaPo); Troy Jackson Will Officially Be Maine’s Democratic Senate Nominee (NOTUS) From the campaign trail Democratic contenders are split over the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s Russia sanctions bill, a bipartisan move to authorize tariffs of up to % on the top five foreign purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas. The legislation doesn’t specify which countries could end up slapped with tariffs, a sticking point for potential White House hopefuls who want to cut into Russia’s financial lifeline but fear it hands Donald Trump too much sweeping power. “Trump has shown himself to abuse tariff authority in a really reckless way that's causing harm to our economy,” Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) told NOTUS’ Igor Bobic . But Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Arizona) said helping Ukraine win is paramount: “There's been a bipartisan effort for almost a year and a half now to pass this bill, and I think that we should pass it and not let the perfect be the enemy of the good.” Latino voters in a handful of congressional districts could determine who wins the House majority, and both parties are fighting over this key voting bloc in Arizona, California, Colorado, New Mexico and Texas. Republicans want to keep Latinos who backed Trump on their side, while Democrats are hoping some have soured on the president and will return to their column. “We can’t be critical of people who voted for Trump,” Rep. Vicente Gonzalez , a Democrat in a tough bid for reelection in Texas’ 34th Congressional District, told NOTUS’ Daniella Diaz . Daniel Garza , president of the Libre Initiative, a conservative Latino advocacy group, said, “We’re hearing a lot that Democrats have failed to give Latino voters something to vote for, that they’re focused more on who to vote against, and that is not good enough.” From the administration Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has long promised to ban drug commercials. But action toward that goal is moving slowly, NOTUS’ Paige Winfield Cunningham reports . What’s more, drugmakers are dropping more cash on the ads than they did a year ago. The top spenders? Makers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, and of drugs to treat psoriasis and Crohn’s disease. From the states Democrats call it honesty, while Republicans call it evidence. title: The DNC Put Up Its Headquarters as Collateral to Obtain Its Massive Loan
author: Elena Schneider, Jasmine Wright
summary: It’s raised concern among members that it’s further evidence of the financial strain the committee is under.
content: Rod Lamkey/AP The Democratic National Committee put its physical headquarters up for collateral last year in order to obtain a $15 million line of credit to help invest in off-year elections, according to D.C. records not previously reported. The building, located in Southeast Washington and partially owned by the DNC, has been used as collateral in the past, including in other election cycles. That the DNC had to do so again ahead of the elections to obtain its biggest-ever off-year loan raised concerns among some members that it was further evidence of its intensifying financial strain. The DNC did not explicitly declare the building as its collateral in its monthly or loan-related filings to the Federal Election Commission. “Ken gaslighting us about the DNC’s finances and not being transparent about the financial situation makes us doubt if he can oversee the DNC during the most important primary of our lifetime,” said a DNC member, granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly. The DNC is working toward two main goals: to help the party win back control of Congress in November, as well as gubernatorial and local elections across the country. And it’s also preparing for the presidential primary, which is expected to be wide open and have no clear front-runner. Those objectives have been complicated by the DNC’s current lack of money. Federal disclosures from June showed it only had about $16 million in its account and $18 million in debt. That’s a sobering amount of money compared to the Republican National Committee, which declared that it had $ million in cash with no outstanding debts. "This is not new,” said a DNC official in a statement about the party using the building as collateral. “The loan documents were publicly released in November, and the DNC's building was also used as collateral in our prior lines of credit in , , , and many other years." Another Democrat close to the DNC said Ken Martin, the beleaguered Democratic Party chair, has struggled to convince donors to maximize their contributions, which has contributed to the small cash-on-hand total. Martin is under particularly close scrutiny. He was the subject of an internal human resources inquiry after throwing a phone in the direction of a young aide in early July, according to five sources who have direct knowledge of the situation or were briefed on the matter. The New York Times first reported the phone-throwing incident. It’s the latest internal flare-up for the chair, who is tasked with reversing the party’s fortunes but faces growing skepticism amid paltry fundraising numbers and a botched release of the election autopsy that almost cost him his position as chair. For some of those sources, the incident with the cellphone reflected a tense mood inside the DNC that has only deepened. The incident occurred after call time, a block in his schedule where Martin would call political allies or donors. While the details of what set Martin off are unclear, multiple people who were briefed on the matter said he got angry and threw his phone in the direction of his aide, though it did not hit the staffer. The incident left a small group of aides who were present shaken and resulted in a human resources inquiry, two of the five sources said. It is unclear who placed the HR inquiry. “It’s just fucking unnacceptable. This is spiraling behavior,” said one DNC source briefed on the incident. Another source who heard about it said it was “not surprising,” given Martin’s recent demeanor. Another source who was familiar with the incident said the phone was thrown at the aide’s desk and not at the aide, which they argued made the incident less severe. All of the sources who spoke to NOTUS requested anonymity for fear of retaliation. Martin, who was elected as DNC chair in February of , apologized to the aide the following business day in a meeting with HR, a DNC source said, and the committee has tried to move past this incident. NOTUS is declining to name the aide involved. The aide did not respond to a request for comment from NOTUS. Martin in the meantime has been on the defensive about the DNC publicly. Last week, he defended the committee’s current financial status as a new strategy in an op-ed on Substack . Responding to criticism of the party’s low cash-on-hand totals, Martin wrote that the DNC has made the “conscious decision” to invest the cash it raises into “electoral assets: more people, earlier organizing, better technology, and stronger state parties.” “That answer may be unsatisfying to people who believe the purpose of a political party is to accumulate the largest possible bank balance until the final days before an election,” Martin said. “But a party is not a savings account. Its purpose is to build power.” Martin also wrote that the DNC has “done exceptionally better with high-net worth donors,” citing an increase of donations from major donors relative to comparable years. The DNC is also grappling with fallout from the changes it wants to make ahead of . On Friday, its rules committee approved a new Democratic presidential calendar — but not before serious sparring among states that wanted to be in the early window. The voting schedule, which has South Carolina voting first, followed by Nevada and New Hampshire, still needs to go before the full DNC for a vote in its August meeting, but already at least two states have made their displeasure at the order public. The pressure of the job, three Democrats close to the DNC told NOTUS, appears to be having an effect on Martin. One of the three sources pointed to the controversy Martin over the incomplete election autopsy in May as the inflection point. NOTUS reported a brewing crisis over Martin’s leadership after the autopsy. It was released with errors and ultimately failed to reach an explanation for what went wrong. It also failed to include an executive summary, even though one was mentioned in the report. The blowback grew contentious — sources NOTUS spoke to at the time said that Martin refusing to share the larger problem of the autopsy with a broader group of officials at the DNC contributed to the outsized reaction. There was even talk of a no confidence vote, though it never came to pass. “He’s been super paranoid,” said one of the DNC sources of Martin’s recent behavior. “He’s super embattled.” That source pointed to the fact that DNC officers were asked to sign nondisclosure agreements in advance of a meeting concerning its financial circumstances as an example. The nondisclosure agreements were first reported by Axios and confirmed by NOTUS. “He’s not in a great place at all,” said one of the sources close to Martin. “I’m very concerned.”

title: Sen. Alan Armstrong Violated STOCK Act With 700 Tardy Stock Disclosures
author: Dave Levinthal
summary: Taken together, the Oklahoma Republican’s financial trades are worth millions of dollars.
content: Armstrong finally disclosed them this week when the House, in a - vote, passed the Republican-sponsored Stop Insider Trading Act, which aims to ban members of Congress from purchasing individual stocks at all. J. Scott Applewhite/AP One of the Senate’s newest members was months late disclosing personal stock trades that together are worth millions of dollars, according to a NOTUS review of new congressional financial records . Sen. Alan Armstrong (R-Oklahoma), who entered the Senate on March 24 after Markwayne Mullin vacated his seat to become homeland security secretary, made a flurry of stock purchases and sales in the several days after his swearing in. But the senator, a wealthy businessman who served as CEO of the oil and gas company Williams Companies until and as executive chairman thereafter , didn’t publicly disclose his financial moves until this week — more than two months past a 45-day deadline mandated by the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act. Together, Armstrong’s improperly disclosed stock trades are worth between $3.24 million and $16.05 million, a NOTUS analysis of the new financial records indicates. (Federal lawmakers are only required to disclose their trades in broad ranges.) Armstrong finally disclosed them this week when the House, in a - vote, passed the Republican-sponsored Stop Insider Trading Act , which aims to ban members of Congress from purchasing individual stocks at all. But it faces an uncertain path through the Senate despite President Donald Trump’s stated support for the legislation. Armstrong’s most valuable stock purchases in late March include at least $ , worth of Apple shares and at least $50, each of Alphabet, Berkshire Hathaway and NVIDIA shares, according to congressional financial records . He also purchased at least $15, worth of stock in each of 70 other companies the week he entered Congress, including federal defense contractors BAE Systems, GE Aerospace, Palantir and RTX. He reported several hundred other stock purchases valued between $1, and $15, each during the week after becoming a senator. The senator was also late to disclose dozens of individual stock sales, including revealing that he sold $ , worth of shares in the glassmaker Corning — a major government contractor — and at least $50, each in companies such as FedEx, Home Depot, oil company Phillips 66 and drugmaker Pfizer. Armstrong this week disclosed only two stock trades within the STOCK Act’s required disclosure window: a June 24 sale of between $5 million and $25 million worth of Williams Companies stock and a June 22 sale of at least $ , worth of Williams Companies stock options. Congress passed the bipartisan STOCK Act in to defend against insider trading, curb lawmaker conflicts of interest and enhance public transparency. Then-President Barack Obama signed it into law. Christine Harbin, an Armstrong spokesperson, acknowledged but did not respond to several questions about the senator’s stock trades, including why he disclosed them after a federal deadline, whether he paid a standard $ fine for late disclosures and if he’s contacted the Senate Ethics Committee to discuss the matter. The Senate Ethics Committee, which acknowledged but did not respond to questions about Armstrong’s stock trades, polices STOCK Act-related matters in Congress’ upper chamber. Asked whether Armstrong’s stock purchases pose a conflict of interest with his public service, Harbin said in an email: “There is no conflict of interest in Senator Armstrong’s intense focus on permitting reform and his long term holding in The Williams Companies stock. In fact, Senator Armstrong sold a significant amount of Williams stock since he was appointed to the position as the referenced filing shows.”A brief, unsigned note appended to Armstrong’s disclosure document states: “Transactions executed in March were initiated by a third party advisor to implement a direct indexing strategy.” Armstrong is barred by Oklahoma law from seeking a Senate term of his own and is slated to leave the Senate in January when a new Congress is seated. He nevertheless joins an ever-growing roster of federal lawmakers who have violated the STOCK Act’s disclosure provisions during the past year, with Reps. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas) and Laurel Lee (R-Florida) also improperly disclosing stock and stock-option trades this week. Others include Sens. Katie Britt (R-Alabama), Susan Collins (R-Maine), John Hickenlooper (D-Colorado), Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota), John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania) and Mullin , whom Armstrong replaced. In the House, STOCK Act violators include Reps. Linda Sánchez (D-California), Julia Letlow (R-Louisiana), Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), Lisa McClain (R-Michigan), Pat Ryan (D-New York), Sheri Biggs (R-South Carolina), Donald Norcross (D-New Jersey), Tim Walberg (R-Michigan), Rich McCormick (R-Georgia), Ritchie Torres (D-New York), Troy Nehls (R-Texas), Dan Meuser (R-Pennsylvania), Jonathan Jackson (D-Illinois), George Whitesides (D-California), Val Hoyle (D-Oregon), Austin Scott (R-Georgia), Shri Thanedar (D-Michigan), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Florida), Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), Kelly Morrison (D-Minnesota), Christian Menefee (D-Texas), Daniel Webster (R-Florida), Ed Case (D-Hawaii) and Scott Franklin (R-Florida). Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma) was also late, although his office denies it.

title: Boosie Badazz’s Estranged MAGA Lobbyists Just Inked a New Trump Pardon Client
author: Taylor Giorno
summary: The rapper has accused Jack Burkman and Jacob Wohl of reneging on a promise to return $ , if they did not quickly secure a pardon.
content: Jack Burkman (left) and Jacob Wohl (right) have signed several clients seeking pardons from President Donald Trump. D M / Creative Commons Another criminal who wants President Donald Trump to pardon him for his financial crimes has hired Jack Burkman and Jacob Wohl — two convicted fraudsters who are facing legal action from rapper Boosie Badazz, a former pardon client who’s accused the duo of misleading him. Burkman and Wohl registered last week to lobby on behalf of Rajendra Parikh, who was sentenced last month to two years in prison for his role in a multimillion-dollar fraud scheme. Judge Deborah Chasanow also ordered Parikh, who pleaded guilty in to conspiracy to commit bank fraud, to forfeit $6 million and pay more than $6 million in restitution. Neither Burkman nor Parikh’s lawyer, Robert Welsh, responded to requests for comment. Burkman and Wohl have signed several clients seeking federal pardons or support on “DOJ issues” since Trump returned to the White House in January . One of their clients, the nursing home mogul Joseph Schwartz, secured a pardon last fall. But as NOTUS reported last week, Boosie, whose legal name is Torence Hatch, is taking legal action against Burkman, Wohl and the firm. BoosieBadazz.1 ( , AR: 1.50)Boosie, who has not received a pardon and terminated his contract with the firm in March, has accused Burkman and Wohl of withholding half of the $ , retainer that the rapper said they agreed to repay if they did not quickly secure a federal pardon, according to a copy of the signed contract reviewed by NOTUS. JM Burkman & Associates previously said in a statement to NOTUS that “no provision to return half the fee was ever actually agreed to.” In text messages reviewed by NOTUS, Burkman told Boosie in March that he and Wohl were “essentially bankrupt.” Burkman and Wohl owe millions of dollars in fines for running an illegal robocall scheme that targeted Black voters in several states, urging them to avoid voting by mail.
